title: How to Become a Cybersecurity Analyst (2026 Guide)
dek: Becoming a cybersecurity analyst usually takes 1 to 2 years: build IT and networking fundamentals, earn an entry-level certification like Security+, get hands-on with labs, and target a junior SOC or IT security role.

intent.primaryKeyword: how to become a cybersecurity analyst

seo.metaTitle: How to Become a Cybersecurity Analyst (2026)
seo.metaDescription: A realistic path to becoming a cybersecurity analyst — the fundamentals, entry-level certifications, hands-on labs, and how to land the first job.

sources.label: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Information Security Analysts, Occupational Outlook Handbook
CISA — Cybersecurity education and career resources

body.richText: A cybersecurity analyst defends an organization's systems and data — monitoring for threats, investigating alerts, and hardening defenses. It is a strong career with excellent official outlook, but it is rarely a true entry-level job. Most analysts get there from an IT or networking foundation first.

Honest expectation-setting: "cybersecurity" is competitive at the entry level despite the talk of a talent shortage. The shortage is real for experienced roles; junior roles still attract many applicants. Fundamentals plus hands-on proof are what get you through the door.

items: Monitoring security tools and triaging alerts (often in a Security Operations Center, or SOC)
Investigating suspicious activity and potential incidents
Applying patches, hardening configurations, and reducing attack surface
Running vulnerability scans and helping prioritize fixes
Documenting findings and communicating risk to non-technical stakeholders

body.text: Step 1 — Build IT and networking fundamentals (2-6 months)

body.richText: You cannot defend what you do not understand. Learn how networks, operating systems, and the basics of how computers talk to each other actually work. Many analysts start in IT support or help desk roles precisely because it builds this foundation and pays you while you learn.

body.text: Step 2 — Earn an entry-level certification (1-3 months)

richText: CompTIA Security+ is the most common entry-level security certification and is widely requested in job postings, including for roles tied to U.S. government work. Read our honest take on whether

body.richText: Certifications prove you can pass an exam; labs prove you can do the work. Build a home lab or use online cyber ranges and capture-the-flag exercises. Being able to talk through something you actually broke and fixed is what wins interviews.

body.text: Step 4 — Target the right first role (varies)

body.richText: Your realistic first title is often SOC analyst (Tier 1), junior security analyst, or an IT role with security responsibilities. Do not hold out only for a "cybersecurity analyst" title — adjacent roles build the same experience and lead to it.

body.caption: Typical time and cost to reach a first cybersecurity analyst role.

body.richText: The official outlook is strong. The BLS projects much-faster-than-average growth for information security analysts — see the numbers in our salary guide.

Not always. Many security professionals enter through IT experience and certifications rather than a security degree. That said, the BLS notes information security analysts typically hold a bachelor's degree in a computer field, and some employers still filter for one. Certifications and hands-on skill can offset the lack of a degree, especially combined with any IT experience.

items.question: Can I become a cybersecurity analyst with no experience?
items.answerRichText: Rarely without any IT background at all. Most people build fundamentals first — often in an IT support role — then add Security+ and hands-on labs. That combination substitutes for direct security experience.

items.question: What certification should I start with for cybersecurity?
answerRichText: CompTIA Security+ is the standard entry point. It is vendor-neutral, widely requested, and requires no prior certification. See whether

link.text: Security+ is worth it for you

items.question: How long does it take to become a cybersecurity analyst?
items.answerRichText: Typically 1 to 2 years for a career-changer building from scratch, or as little as 6 to 18 months if you already have IT or networking experience to build on.
